children: By Deborah Acosta

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla.-Venture-capital powerhouse Andreessen Horowitz is launching a new regional headquarters in South Florida, focusing on defense investments two years after it fled the region following a short-lived crypto office in Miami.

The Menlo Park, Ca.-based firm said it is planning to open its new base next year in West Palm Beach, where a team will oversee the American Dynamism fund. That vehicle has raised $1.18 billion for startups building technologies for national security and the industrial economy.

Florida is emerging as a major hub for companies financing the burgeoning new defense business, which is increasingly turning to startups as artificial intelligence and drone warfare reshape the battlefield.

The state is home to the three headquarters that plan and coordinate military operations across Latin America, the Middle East and special global operations. The state also hosts the nation's premier national-security launch complexes up and down the Space Coast along the Atlantic in Central Florida. Florida also features a concentration of government institutions that buy defense equipment and a growing pool of wealthy investors.

Florida's embrace of the defense industry is part of a growing shift in the state's economic identity, notably after Miami pulled back from previous efforts to position itself as the world's crypto capital.
Gov. Ron DeSantis last week said the state was investing nearly $23 million to strengthen the state's defense industrial base, pushing to capture a portion of the defense tech boom.

Florida offers a "suite of unmatched financial tools" that lower the cost of capital through tax savings and other measures, said Rob Long, chief executive of Space Florida, the state's aerospace finance, development and spaceport authority.

Overall, Florida's military and defense industry generates $102.6 billion in economic impact and supports more than 865,000 jobs statewide, according to the Florida Defense Industry Economic Impact Analysis.

Space and defense-oriented startups have begun to pop up in South Florida, too, including Space-Eyes, a geospatial intelligence and counterdrone technology company that recently brought on Eric Trump as an investor and strategic adviser. Satellite manufacturer Terran Orbital built out its South Florida footprint before it was acquired by Lockheed Martin in 2024.
The sheer number of defense-tech startups based in Florida is still relatively small, trailing bigger hubs like Northern and Southern California.

But defense companies are increasingly coming to raise money, make connections and get in front of the military and national-security officials who live and work there, including Pentagon leaders like Emil Michael, who oversees the department's AI efforts and lives in Miami.
Andreessen Horowitz is part of that budding movement. The early stage venture-capital firm is devoting a bigger chunk of its focus into the growing defense tech space nationally.
The firm made an early bet on Miami's burgeoning crypto economy, opening a Miami office only to close it two years later when the local crypto market tanked.
Katherine Boyle, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz and co-founder of the firm's American Dynamism practice, said she has higher hopes for investing in defense startups in the state.

"We've seen capital move to Florida in the last five years in droves," said Boyle. "It really is this incredible ecosystem and city that's been built up over the last several years, and it's become an important nexus for space, military and funding."

Stephen Ross, the real-estate veteran and the biggest developer in West Palm Beach who courted Andreessen, thinks the VC firm's move "shows young people this is a place where they can start up businesses and grow in an environment that really perpetuates growth."
It's not alone. Palantir, the data-mining giant deeply entrenched in federal defense contracts, also recently relocated its global headquarters to Miami.

Florida's military importance began with geography. Its position at the country's southern maritime gateway and its proximity to the Caribbean and Latin America enabled it to accumulate military importance over decades as new military missions were layered onto that strategic foundation.

Academia is also rushing to meet this convergence of capital and defense. Vanderbilt University is expanding plans for a graduate campus in West Palm Beach, from 1,000 to 2,000 students, and will include defense tech and national-security studies in the context of space, energy and infrastructure.

The Trump administration has also worked to facilitate these initiatives, including by proposing ways for space companies to avoid environmental reviews, and also by facilitating more defense contracts between startups and the Pentagon.
